listeningScripts.title: Bank Account Fraud Alert
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, I'm calling about suspicious transactions on my account. Bank Officer: I'm sorry to hear that. I'm here to help. Can I have your account number? Customer: It's 5834-291-7465. Over the last three days, I've noticed four withdrawals totaling $1,800 that I didn't make. Officer: Let me pull that up. What are the dates of these transactions? Customer: June 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and today, June 4th. Each one is $450. Officer: I see them all here. These are ATM withdrawals, all from a machine on Bloor Street in Toronto. Are you in Toronto? Customer: No, I'm in Montreal. I haven't been to Toronto in months. Officer: That's definitely suspicious. I'm going to freeze your account immediately to prevent further unauthorized transactions. Customer: What about the money that's already been withdrawn? Officer: We'll file a fraud claim. You're not responsible for unauthorized transactions under the bank's protection policy. You should see a credit back within 5 to 7 business days. Customer: Good. What should I do next? Officer: We'll mail you a new debit card as a precaution, but don't worry about the PIN. I'm also recommending you change your online banking password right away. We'll monitor your account closely. Customer: Should I change my passwords for other accounts too? Officer: That's a wise precaution. Since someone had your card number, they might try other services. Better safe than sorry.

listeningScripts.title: Coffee Shop Catch-Up
listeningScripts.text: Sarah: Hey, how are you? It's been ages! Michael: I know, right? Must be like six months since we last hung out. Sarah: At least. How was your trip to Vancouver? Michael: It was amazing! The weather was beautiful, and I got to see the mountains every day. Sarah: That sounds incredible. Did you do any hiking? Michael: Yeah, we went up to Whistler for a weekend. The views were unbelievable. Sarah: I'm so jealous. I've been meaning to get out there. Hey, do you want to go grab dinner next week? Michael: Absolutely, I'd love that. How about Thursday? Sarah: Thursday works for me. There's that new Italian place downtown that opened last month. Michael: Perfect. Should we book a table? Sarah: Yeah, probably a good idea. What time? Michael: How about 7 PM? Sarah: Sounds good. I'll make the reservation.

listeningScripts.title: University Orientation: First Week Checklist
listeningScripts.text: Hello, welcome to orientation week. I'm here to walk you through essential tasks for your first week. First, attend your faculty's orientation meeting on Monday at ten AM in the Student Centre. Bring your student ID. Second, register for your courses online by Wednesday, August 28th. Early registration means better class times. Third, purchase your textbooks from the university bookstore before classes start. Fourth, get your student photo ID taken at the Services Office between 9 and 4 on any day this week. The photo ID is required for library access and residence entry. Fifth, activate your email account at the IT support desk. Your email is your primary communication channel for all university announcements. Sixth, find your classes on a campus map. Most buildings are located around the central quad. Seventh, attend the Welcome Social on Friday evening in the gymnasium. It's a great way to meet other students and faculty. Eighth, complete your health and immunization form at Student Health Services. This is mandatory before attending classes. Finally, budget about three hundred dollars for books and materials. Questions? Visit the information desk in the main foyer.

listeningScripts.title: Winnipeg Public Transit Modernization
listeningScripts.text: Winnipeg is modernizing its public transit system with a 450 million dollar investment over the next decade. The city has approved plans to purchase 300 new electric buses to replace aging diesel vehicles. The transition will eliminate approximately 8,500 tonnes of annual carbon emissions from the transportation sector. Current ridership stands at 89 million trips annually, and the city expects this to grow by 20 percent once new services launch. Construction of a new rapid transit corridor connecting downtown to the airport is set to begin next year. This corridor will reduce travel time from downtown to the airport from 45 minutes to just 22 minutes. The project includes the construction of 12 new transit stations along the corridor. Free transit passes will be offered to seniors and students to encourage ridership. Overall, the modernization is expected to create 1,100 permanent jobs in operations and maintenance. Winnipeg Transit has committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2040.

listeningScripts.title: University Program Expansion Planning
listeningScripts.text:
Dean Robert: We've been asked to consider expanding our engineering program, particularly in renewable energy studies. The faculty has requested three additional full-time instructors and funding for new laboratory equipment. The cost would be approximately 2.4 million dollars over two years. Given our current budget constraints, I'm hesitant to commit to this expansion.

Professor Elena: I understand the budget concerns, Dean, but we're actually losing enrollment to competing universities who offer these programs. Last year, we lost 150 potential engineering students to schools with stronger renewable energy options. If we don't expand now, we'll fall behind. Plus, there's significant industry demand for graduates with renewable energy expertise. Companies are specifically recruiting from universities with these specialized programs.

Student Representative Malik: From a student perspective, I absolutely support this expansion. Many of my classmates are interested in sustainability and green technology, but we don't have the courses or facilities to support that focus. I think this investment would make our university much more attractive to prospective students, which would actually increase our overall enrollment and revenue.

Budget Committee Member Diana: Malik makes a good point about revenue. If this program attracts even 200 additional students, the tuition revenue would exceed the expansion costs within three years. And we could explore partnerships with industry for funding. I've been in conversations with several renewable energy companies that might contribute equipment or funding in exchange for access to our graduates for recruitment.

listeningScripts.title: Algorithmic Bias in Hiring Systems
listeningScripts.text: Algorithmic bias in hiring is a serious problem that companies are using as a shortcut without taking responsibility for the consequences. Many organizations now use AI systems to screen resumes, assess candidate fit, and predict job performance. These systems seem objective—they're just mathematics, right? Wrong. These algorithms are trained on historical data, which includes decades of human bias. If women were historically excluded from leadership positions, the algorithm learns that pattern and replicates it. If certain demographics were underrepresented in technical roles, the algorithm reinforces that exclusion. Studies have documented this repeatedly. Amazon famously scrapped their hiring algorithm when they discovered it was discriminating against women. Google's recruiting algorithm showed bias against applicants from historically black colleges. These weren't intentional—that's precisely the problem. The systems' creators didn't set out to discriminate; they just trusted that math was unbiased, when in reality, data is never neutral. My argument is this: companies should not deploy algorithmic hiring systems without rigorous bias testing and external auditing. If you use an algorithm to screen candidates, you're making a business decision, and you're responsible for its outcomes. You can't hide behind the algorithm or claim you didn't know it was biased. Moreover, algorithms eliminate human judgment, nuance, and chance. They can't capture potential, resilience, or growth. Some of the most successful employees wouldn't have passed an algorithm. We need a return to more human-centered hiring while using algorithms cautiously and with oversight.
